title: Beyond Static Leaderboards for Agents
hook: Topping an agent leaderboard doesn't mean it'll work when deployed: aggregate-score rankings don't transfer out-of-distribution. Rank by predictive validity instead.
key_points: No single agent benchmark covers more than four or five of the dimensions real deployment exposes.
Rankings from aggregate scores don't transfer to out-of-distribution settings — public-to-hidden retrospectives show rank instability.
Proposes ranking by predictive validity: the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank, not the in-sample mean.
Aggregates 14 parallel studies plus 7 prior benchmarks into a 12-tier apparatus exposing dimensions HELM-style leaderboards collapse.
content_html: Agent benchmarks are multiplying fast, but they all share a blind spot: no single one touches more than four or five of the many dimensions that deployment actually exposes. This position paper argues that the standard move — collapse everything into an aggregate score and rank — quietly breaks down when agents leave the lab.
extra_html:
The argument

Drawing on fourteen parallel deep-dive studies of an MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark plus seven prior benchmarks, the authors show that aggregate-score rankings don't transfer to out-of-distribution settings, with public-to-hidden competition retrospectives offering direct evidence of rank instability. Their fix: rank configurations by predictive validity — the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank — rather than by in-sample mean. They lay out a twelve-tier measurement apparatus that surfaces deployment-relevant dimensions which HELM-style leaderboards collapse, and operationalize the position with three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria.

Why it matters

As agents move into production, "which model tops the leaderboard?" is the wrong question if that ranking doesn't survive distribution shift. Predictive validity reframes evaluation around what teams actually care about — will this configuration still win on cases it hasn't seen? — and gives benchmark designers a concrete target to report. The authors are careful that existing evidence only partly supports the claim, and close with a pre-registered pilot.

related.title: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
related.hook: A single accuracy number hides a lot. HELM evaluates language models across many scenarios and many metrics at once — and reports it all in the open.

related.title: Chatbot Arena: Ranking LLMs by Human Preference
related.hook: How do you rank chatbots when there's no single right answer? Let people pick the better of two anonymous replies, then aggregate the votes into a leaderboard.

related.title: EvoArena: Testing Agents in Environments That Keep Changing
related.hook: Most agent benchmarks freeze the world. EvoArena makes the environment keep updating beneath the agent — and finds today's agents crack, averaging under 40%.

related.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability?
related.hook: An agent score only means something if the task still requires the skill it claims to test. Auditing 2,385 traces, two-thirds showed the agent taking a shortcut instead.

flashcards.prompt: What is 'predictive validity' as a way to rank agent configurations?
flashcards.back_html: The correlation between a configuration's in-sample rank and its out-of-sample rank — measuring whether a leaderboard position actually predicts performance on unseen, deployment-like settings, rather than just reporting the in-sample mean.

flashcards.prompt: What core problem does the paper identify with aggregate-score agent leaderboards?

choices.text: Their rankings don't transfer to out-of-distribution, deployment-relevant settings
They are too expensive to compute
They only work for vision models

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors argue aggregate scores systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation; public-to-hidden competition retrospectives provide direct evidence that ranks are unstable out-of-distribution.
